headline: Deadly floods hit the mountains of Nepal

sources.title: Nepal Flash Floods Leave Over 380 Dead and Hundreds More Missing (Time)
Floods kill more than 500 people in Nepal and Tibet (NPR)
2026 Nepal Debris Avalanche and Flash Flood (U.S. Geological Survey)
Nepal flash flood: dramatic footage shows Rasuwa valley engulfed (video, Euronews)

chunks.text: It began high in the mountains, where almost nobody was watching. On Wednesday, August 26, a huge mass of ice and rock {{broke off}} a [[mountainside]] in a national park near Nepal's [[border]] with China. Within minutes, the frozen wall {{came down}} into the [[valley]] below and {{set off}} a giant [[flood]] of mud, water, and stone. A wall of water nearly 30 feet high {{swept away}} houses, bridges, and roads along two rivers.

verbs.correct: To separate from a larger piece
verbs.why: Icebergs break off glaciers, and branches break off trees in storms. Here a mass of ice and rock broke off a mountainside above the valley.
Old walls come down, heavy rain comes down, and power lines come down in storms. The frozen wall came down into the valley within minutes.

verbs.wrong: To measure the size of a quake
verbs.why: A spark can set off a fire, and one rumor can set off a panic. The falling ice set off a giant flood of mud, water, and stone.

verbs.correct: To take something with rushing water
verbs.wrong: To bury something under dry snow
verbs.why: Rivers sweep away cars, and big waves sweep away beach houses. The wall of water swept away homes, bridges, and roads along two rivers.

chunks.text: Scientists thousands of miles away {{picked up}} the shaking. The collapse [[released]] as much energy as a magnitude 5.2 [[earthquake]], according to the United States Geological Survey, and the flood then traveled about 62 miles [[downstream]]. Experts are still not sure exactly why the [[glacier]] failed, but warm weather and heavy rain both weaken mountain ice. The same region was hit by a [[deadly]] [[avalanche]] after the 2015 earthquake.

verbs.correct: To notice a sound or signal
verbs.why: Radios pick up distant stations, and sensors pick up small movements in the ground. Scientists thousands of miles away picked up the shaking from the collapse.

chunks.text: The human cost is [[enormous]], and it is still growing. By Friday, [[officials]] had counted more than 540 deaths in Nepal, and about 1,500 people were still [[missing]], more than half of them foreigners. Among them were more than 100 Indian [[pilgrims]] traveling to a [[holy]] mountain, and dozens of Americans. Whole villages were {{cut off}} from the outside world when the flood destroyed the bridges and the [[main highway]] to China. Rescue helicopters {{pulled out}} more than 120 people, but many places were impossible to reach, and the [[death toll]] was expected to {{go up}}.

verbs.correct: To separate a place from outside help
verbs.wrong: To warn a place about danger
verbs.why: Heavy snow can cut off mountain towns, and floods cut off whole islands. Villages here were cut off when the water destroyed the bridges and the main highway.

verbs.correct: To take someone from a dangerous place
verbs.wrong: To search a building for people
verbs.why: Firefighters pull people out of burning houses, and lifeguards pull swimmers out of the sea. Helicopters pulled out more than 120 people from the flood zone.

verbs.correct: To rise to a higher number
verbs.wrong: To stay the same for weeks
verbs.why: Prices go up, temperatures go up, and rents go up every year. Sadly, officials expected the death toll to go up as rescuers reached more villages.

chunks.text: More than 4,000 police officers joined the [[search]], and [[rescuers]] {{dug out}} [[survivors]] from the mud. The work is dangerous. Teams had to {{call off}} operations for a time when a new lake, formed by the [[debris]], began to [[overflow]]. Foreign governments have {{reached out}} to offer help, but [[aid]] cannot {{get through}} to villages without roads. For families waiting for news, every hour matters.

verbs.correct: To free someone from mud or snow
verbs.wrong: To carry food to a village
verbs.why: Rescue dogs help dig out skiers after an avalanche, and neighbors dig out cars after a snowstorm. Rescuers dug out survivors from the deep mud.

verbs.correct: To stop something that was planned
verbs.wrong: To shout to people far away
verbs.why: Schools call off classes in bad weather, and couples sometimes call off a wedding. Teams had to call off the search when a new lake began to overflow.

verbs.correct: To make contact to offer help
verbs.wrong: To fly over a flooded area
verbs.why: Charities reach out to homeless families, and old friends reach out after a disaster. Foreign governments reached out to Nepal with offers of aid.

verbs.correct: To reach a place despite problems
verbs.wrong: To build a bridge over a river
verbs.why: Supply trucks get through after storms, and letters get through even in wartime. With the roads gone, aid cannot get through to the cut villages.

mainIdea.s: Falling ice and rock started a huge flood in Nepal's mountains that killed hundreds and left many more missing. Rescuers struggle to reach villages that lost their roads and bridges.
mainIdea.why: The collapse set off a flood that killed over 540 people, and cut off villages are still waiting for help.

mainIdea.s: Weeks of heavy monsoon rain slowly raised Nepal's rivers until they finally flooded hundreds of villages. Officials say early warnings helped almost all of the foreign tourists escape.
mainIdea.why: Close, but this was a sudden collapse of ice and rock, not slow rain, and hundreds of foreigners are among the missing.

mainIdea.s: A strong earthquake in the mountains of Nepal destroyed roads and bridges near the border with China. Neighboring countries have sent rescue teams to search the fallen buildings there.
mainIdea.why: There was no earthquake this time. The collapse only released as much energy as one, which is how scientists noticed it.

tf.s: A mass of ice and rock broke off a mountainside and set off the flood
tf.why: It fell in a national park near the border with China, and the flood followed within minutes.

tf.s: Scientists far away picked up the shaking from the collapse
tf.why: The event released as much energy as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, according to the USGS.

tf.s: All of the missing people are citizens of Nepal
tf.why: More than half of the roughly 1,500 missing are foreigners, including Indian pilgrims and dozens of Americans.

tf.s: Some villages were cut off because bridges and the main highway were destroyed
tf.why: That is why aid cannot get through to many places, even though helicopters pulled out more than 120 people.

tf.s: The rescue teams have never had to stop their work
tf.why: They had to call off operations for a time when a lake formed by the debris began to overflow.

tf.s: Officials expected the death toll to go up
tf.why: By Friday more than 540 deaths were counted in Nepal, with many areas still impossible to reach.

lines.text: Did you see the story about the floods in Nepal?
I did. [[That's awful]]. It started with a glacier, didn't it?
Yes. A huge piece of ice and rock {{broke off}} a mountain near the Chinese border. It {{came down}} into the valley in minutes and {{set off}} a flood of mud, water, and stone.
And the flood {{swept away}} whole villages. Houses, bridges, roads. [[I can't imagine]] being there.
[[Honestly]], neither can I. Scientists thousands of miles away {{picked up}} the shaking. It was like a small earthquake.
I read that. And the number of deaths is still {{going up}}?
Yes. More than 540 so far, and about 1,500 people are missing. Many of them were foreign visitors.
[[The worst part is]] the villages nobody can reach. The flood {{cut off}} the whole area when the bridges were destroyed.
Helicopters have {{pulled out}} more than a hundred people, but a lot of places are still impossible to reach.
And the rescuers on the ground are {{digging out}} survivors from the mud with their hands. That must be so dangerous.
It is. They had to {{call off}} the search for a while because a new lake started to overflow.
[[Makes sense]]. They can't risk losing the rescue teams too.
Other countries have {{reached out}} to offer help, but the aid can't {{get through}} to the villages without roads.
So the families just have to wait. Do you think more help will arrive in time?
[[I hope so]]. Every hour matters for those families.

expressions.def: Used to show that you are shocked or very sad about something bad that has happened.
ex: She lost her job and her apartment in the same week? That's awful.
That's awful. Is his family okay?

expressions.def: Used to say that something is so terrible or so extreme that you cannot picture what it would be like.
ex: I can't imagine losing everything in one night.
Three days without water? I can't imagine.

expressions.def: Used before a statement to show that you are giving your true feelings or opinion.
ex: Honestly, I was too upset to sleep after the news.
Honestly, I don't know what I would do in that situation.

expressions.def: Used to introduce the most upsetting or serious part of a bad situation.
ex: The worst part is that nobody warned them.
The worst part is the waiting. The families still don't know anything.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is logical or that you understand why it was done.
ex: They closed the road because of the ice. Makes sense.
Makes sense. It's too dangerous to work there at night.

expressions.def: Used to say that you want something to be true or to happen, but you are not sure it will.
ex: Will the rain stop before the weekend? I hope so.
I hope so. They really need the supplies.
